newsitem.title: CANADA: AIR CANADA SAYS FLEET PLAN WON'T HIT CARGO.
newsitem.headline: AIR CANADA SAYS FLEET PLAN WON'T HIT CARGO.

text.p: Air Canada's plan to retire its Boeing 747 combi fleet will not have a major impact on cargo customers for several years, if at all, said Bob Thomson, managing director of Air Canada Cargo.

With six combis all on the North Atlantic now, the airline "is hard-pressed to fill" all the 747 main deck capacity it has. Even after retiring three of the six after 1999, it will have adequate main deck lift, he told Reuters by telephone from Montreal.
"By removing the (first three) we still will have a good Atlantic product,"
With only three combis, Air Canada still would have as much main deck capacity on the North Atlantic as it did two years ago, when some of the 747s were flying the Pacific.

Air Canada has ordered up to 28 Airbus Industrie A330/340 widebodies to replace its nine combi and all-passenger 747s. The carrier's fleet plan calls for the last three combis to leave the fleet by 2002, leaving the airline with no main-deck cargo product.
The 747 combi is a mixed configuration aircraft with more than double the cargo capacity of a passenger 747.
Some customers book Air Canada to access that main deck space on the combis for freight too large or wide to move in the belly of passenger aircraft.
If Air Canada has no main deck capacity, some argue that it will lose those customers altogether.
Thomson said on some routes, being able to offer upper deck space does get belly freight from the same customers, Thomson said.
"You'll tend to broker the upper deck" by tying it to lower deck business, he said. "However, I don't think we would lose any particular customer because we didn't have main deck (capacity)."
If it becomes necessary, the airline could reach space sharing agreements with freighter operators to provide main deck space.
The airline's fleet analysis leading up to the Airbus order factored in possible cargo revenue losses, he said.

All things considered, the cost savings and other benefits from replacing the 747s with A330/340s: "simply outweighed the value of the upper deck", Thomson added. "It's an opportunity we had to take."

Replacing 747s with A330s will result in a net reduction of space. The 17-tonne belly capacity of an A330 is less than half of the 39-42 tonne cargo capacity of a 747 combi, but more than the 14 tonnes carried on passenger 747-100s, which are also being retired.

"Being realistic, it's about the best that could happen. And in 2-3 years time (when the final decision on the 747-400s is to be made), who knows what could happen?" said Thomson. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
